title: Air Plan Approval; Colorado; Inspection and Maintenance Program Revision
summary:
The Environmental Protection Agency has finalized Colorado’s updates to its motor vehicle emissions inspection program, with the changes taking effect December 18, 2025. The agency also noted a separate, administrative update acknowledging Montana’s earlier certification that its clean air plan addresses the 2015 ozone standard.

In Colorado, the approval covers a broad refresh of “Regulation Number 11,” which governs how cars and trucks are tested and how the program is run. It includes updated definitions and applicability, adds more detail to remote “clean screen” options that can clear well‑performing vehicles without a traditional inspection, clarifies procedures for exhaust and emissions control checks (including engine changes), and updates the licensing and training rules for inspectors, mechanics, facilities, and dealer test sites. The enhanced inspection program is also affirmed for the North Front Range. EPA concluded these revisions will not reduce the program’s emission‑cutting benefits and are consistent with the Clean Air Act. No public comments were submitted on the proposal, and the federal action does not add requirements beyond state law.

Who stands to benefit? Front Range communities and anyone sensitive to air pollution may see continued progress on ozone and related pollutants. Drivers with cleaner vehicles could gain convenience from expanded remote testing options. Repair shops and technicians get clearer, updated standards that can improve consistency and consumer confidence. State and local air agencies gain a federally backed rule set that’s enforceable and easier to administer.

Who might be negatively affected? Some motorists will still face the time and cost of inspections and necessary repairs, and certain stations or repair businesses may need to adjust processes, training, or equipment to meet the updated rules. While EPA determined the changes don’t create significant new costs for small businesses and don’t impose new federal burdens, any program update can mean short‑term adjustments.

Overall, this is a maintenance and modernization step: Colorado keeps its vehicle testing program aligned with today’s air quality needs and technologies, with federal approval confirming the state’s approach without layering on new federal mandates.
